opus-5.5.text:
I think it's honestly one of the best times there's ever been to learn to code. The barrier to getting started has dropped dramatically. When I was learning, you'd spend hours stuck on some obscure error message or fighting with your environment before you ever got to build anything interesting. Now you have this incredibly patient collaborator sitting right next to you that can explain what's going on, suggest a fix, and, importantly, tell you *why* it works.

But I'd push back a little on the idea that AI means you don't need to understand code anymore. What's actually happening is that the leverage you get from understanding code has gone up. If you know what good software looks like, how systems fit together, how to read a diff and spot when something's off, you can direct these agents to do far more than you ever could alone. You become something closer to a tech lead for a team of very fast, very capable collaborators. And the people who get the most out of tools like Codex are the ones who can reason about the architecture, give clear intent, and review the output critically.

The other thing I'd say is that the feedback loop is so much tighter now. You can have an idea in the morning and a working prototype by lunch. That kind of fast iteration is how people really learn. You try something, you see it work or break, you ask questions, you go deeper. AI makes that loop almost frictionless, so curiosity gets rewarded much faster.

So my advice is: learn to code, but learn it alongside these tools. Use them to go deeper, not to skip understanding. Ask the model to explain things, challenge it, read what it writes. If you do that, you'll learn faster than any generation of programmers before you, and you'll be able to build things that would have taken whole teams not long ago.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can make learning and iteration faster, but does not specifically say Codex accelerates learning an unfamiliar programming language.

r002.rationale: It does not describe Codex directing learners to established solutions instead of reinventing standard programming functionality.

r003.rationale: It says learners can ask questions, but does not state that Codex can surface questions they do not yet know to ask.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's worthwhile now because the barrier between having an idea and seeing it work has basically collapsed. A few years ago, learning to code meant spending months on syntax, on setup, on all the friction before you could build anything real. Now you can sit down with a model, describe what you want, and have something running in minutes. And that changes what learning is for.

What I'd say to people is: the skill that matters is less about memorizing how to write a for loop and more about understanding what you're building. Knowing how systems fit together, knowing what good looks like, being able to read what the model produced and say "no, that's not quite right, here's why." The model handles a lot of the mechanical work, so your attention goes to the judgment part. And that's actually the more interesting part of engineering anyway.

There's also a window right now where the people who learn to work this way are going to compound faster than everyone else. The tools are getting better month over month. If you start today, you're building intuition for how to direct these systems, where they're reliable, where they drift, how to break a problem into pieces an agent can handle well. That intuition carries forward even as the models change underneath you.

And honestly, it's just more fun. You spend less time stuck on a missing semicolon and more time actually making things. For someone who's always been curious about building software but got discouraged by the early grind, there's never been a better moment to try again.

astra-6.text:
I think AI makes it much easier to get started. When you’re learning to code, you often have an idea of what you want to build, but you get stuck on something small. Now you can ask for an explanation, try a fix, and keep moving. You can learn in the context of something you actually care about building.

And learning to code helps you get more out of AI, too. You can describe what you want more precisely, understand the choices it makes, and check whether the result actually works. So even as the tools get better at writing code, understanding software gives you more control over what you can create.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s worthwhile because the distance between having an idea and being able to build it is shrinking so quickly. You can start with something you actually want to make, ask the AI to help, and learn along the way. When you get stuck, you can ask it to explain an error, walk through a piece of code, or show you another approach.

But learning to code still matters. It gives you the ability to understand what the AI is doing, judge whether it’s right, and guide it toward what you want. You don’t have to learn everything before you can make something useful. You can build and learn at the same time, and that’s a really exciting way to get started.
